title: "Is “Shiloh” a name meaning “One Sent”?"
description: "An examination of Genesis 49:10 and the claim: Genesis 49:10 calls the coming Messiah “Shiloh,” understood as “One Sent,” and John 17:3 fulfils this title by describing Jesus as sent by God."

summary: "Genesis’s disputed word and John’s language of sending can be linked devotionally. Do they establish a predicted name?"
ot_reference: "Gen 49:10"
ot_text_url: "https://ebible.org/engbsb/GEN49.htm#V10"
ot_text: "The scepter will not depart from Judah, nor the staff from between his feet, until Shiloh comes and the allegiance of the nations is his."
ot_note: "Or from his descendants Or until the one to whom tribute belongs"
christian_case: "The BSB’s main text presents Shiloh as someone who comes and receives the allegiance of nations. Together with early Jewish messianic reception, this permits a Christian identification of the coming ruler with Jesus. The shared audit associates the “sent” interpretation with the Vulgate’s rendering, and John 17:3 explicitly describes Jesus as sent by God. That translation tradition supplies a route for the Christian association, even though the Hebrew derivation remains a separate question."
critical_case: "The central phrase has several substantial competing readings, including tribute and rightful possession. No biblical text independently establishes Shiloh as a name for the Messiah. The audit specifically rejects “sent” as a secure Hebrew etymology and associates it with the Vulgate’s rendering. John 17:3 uses ordinary mission language: it neither calls Jesus Shiloh nor cites Genesis 49:10. A traditional translation association therefore cannot establish the asserted Hebrew name prediction."
verdict_label: "Disputed title; unsupported “One Sent” equation"
verdict: "Reading Shiloh messianically is a possible interpretation within a genuine messianic reception history. Calling it a predicted name meaning “One Sent” goes further than the linguistic evidence, and John 17:3 does not supply the missing identification."
